main_argument_chains.claim: Past crime locations can produce a prioritized home-search field when linkage, one-base, and distance-decay assumptions are plausible.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Use the map as a search ordering, not as calibrated probability, and screen excluded geographies and offender behaviors first.

main_argument_chains.claim: A candidate next crime can be ranked by how its insertion changes the inferred home field.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Repair score direction and buffer-domain contradictions before allocating prevention resources.

main_argument_chains.claim: Recency weighting can reveal movement only when time and location are associated.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Calibrate and validate multiple time models rather than assuming coupling always helps.
Require case diagnostics, abstention, complete plots, and external rolling evaluation before deployment.

warnings.warning: The mean-center equations are called averages but omit division by the total weight; taking every w_i=1 yields coordinate sums rather than a center unless normalized weights are silently assumed.
The 68 percent and 95 percent SDC coverage statements require a distributional interpretation that is not derived for these spatial point patterns.
The circle-hypothesis evidence for serial rapists is generalized to serial murder and other criminal types without a direct transfer validation.
One offender and exactly one home base are assumed, excluding linkage uncertainty, multiple anchors, and mobile or commuter behavior.
Terrain, road access, population density, opportunity, and inhabitable-area constraints are omitted, so high-score cells can be operationally impossible.
Euclidean calculations on latitude and longitude are not accompanied by a projection, spherical-distance rule, or unit conversion.
Linear, Normal, exponential, truncated, and plateau kernel parameters are not reported in a reproducible calibration table.
The additive normalized field is called a criminal-location probability although no generative likelihood, prior, or calibration test supports that interpretation.
Finer meshes are said to approximate an ideal smooth solution, but no resolution sensitivity or convergence diagnostic is shown.
The concrete 2 GHz runtime and 36 by 36 meter England-grid claim has no implementation, benchmark log, memory use, or kernel specification.

The prose says lower squared distribution deviation means a more likely next crime, but Programs 2 and 3 normalize the deviation without reversing its order, so larger deviations receive larger returned values.
The prose says virtual crimes are not added in the buffer, yet Programs 2 and 3 iterate candidate g over the augmented grid G prime rather than the interior G.
Program 2 specifies a 40 percent boundary buffer, whereas Figure 3 and Program 3 use 30 percent.
The O(n^4) next-crime complexity collapses a two-dimensional n by m grid to one symbol and does not state the effect of crime count or buffer size.
The claimed factor-N caching speedup and normalization-preserving combination are not derived or benchmarked.
Near-perfect parallel speedup equal to the number of cores ignores communication, memory bandwidth, scheduling, and aggregation overhead.
With observed times t_1 through t_(N-1), the mean of the N-2 observed intervals normally has denominator N-2, not the paper's N-1.
The time method is called linear regression, but the displayed rule is a one-step average-span extrapolation with no fitted regression line or residual analysis.
Parameters a, c, and d in the time-weighting function are undefined and no fit, units, or sensitivity analysis is reported.
Only one time-weight family is studied in depth and the synthetic correlated/uncorrelated experiment omits seeds, sample size, Poisson rate, parameter values, and repeated-run uncertainty.
The validation withholds only the most recent event from two main case datasets rather than using rolling origins, an external set, or repeated cross-validation.
Search Cost tie handling is described only as no preference within the same color, leaving exact rank treatment and color-bin effects unspecified.
Table 1 does not label Search Cost as percent versus fraction and does not state the distance units for Error Distance.
Kernel and time-weight choices are developed and evaluated on the same small case collection, creating tuning and selection optimism.
Time coupling generally worsens the reported values, but the paper offers no statistical test and initially attributes the behavior to bad luck.
The conclusion extrapolates Sutcliffe performance to larger datasets without evidence that more data, different offenders, or different geographies preserve accuracy.
Jack the Ripper dates are printed as 1988 in Appendix A but as 1888 in the preceding date table.
Panel (l) is titled Next Crime Location Probability but its caption calls it a Criminal Location plot.
The page headed Model Plots for Chester Turner actually repeats Sutcliffe coordinates, data, and captions, so the promised Turner visual comparison is absent.
The references contain suspicious pagination, misspellings, and inconsistent bibliographic formatting, limiting reproducibility.

Shows the complete input-method-metric-result-output chain on one page.
Places single-offender, single-base, commuter, terrain, and population limits before strengths.
Connects red, yellow, and blue bands to search and prevention actions and reports runtime scale.
Confirms the full route, appendix, and 33-page structure.
Establishes expected centers, spread, boundaries, and next-event ambiguity.
Shows directional spread and two-hotspot expectations that a credible field should preserve.
Contrasts Linear, Normal, Negative Exponential, and Truncated Negative Exponential shapes on common axes.
Overlays observed crimes and the actual base on a longitude-latitude heat map.
Makes grid iteration, additive kernel evaluation, normalization, and output explicit.
Demonstrates automatic multimodal hotspots without an external clustering stage.
Exposes the augmented grid, virtual-event loop, sum-squared deviation, and returned field.
Shows the edge artifact without a buffer and the changed field with a 30 percent buffer.
Compares the predicted withheld event in red with the actual event in black.
Shows how the time weight enters both home and future-crime algorithms.
Displays a fall from roughly 10 at day zero toward 2 by day 100.
Contrasts weighted and unweighted next-crime fields for correlated and uncorrelated synthetic timings.
Shows criminal-location fields changing less rapidly than next-crime fields under correlated motion.
Reports exact Search Cost / Error Distance pairs for five kernels, two targets, two coupling modes, and two offenders.
Displays timing error for five offenders without a caption or stated unit metric.
Preserves 52 latitude-longitude-date rows for five offender series and source attribution.
Compares home and next-crime fields under the linear kernel on common coordinates.
Shows how tail and buffer behavior change home and next-crime hotspots.
Shows alternative buffer assumptions on the same crime pattern.
Shows the recency-weighted home and next-crime outputs.
